reasons.evidence: In the 2 earlier years of data, Cabbage prices around the target date were 16.9% below prices around the forecast start (October to December); 2 of 2 years moved that way.
reasons.meaning: The model's seasonal pattern pushed this forecast lower, in line with what earlier years show.

reasons.title: Price compared with its usual level
reasons.evidence: Same time last year: the starting price of ₹1,300 per quintal is 44% above its median over the past year (₹900).
reasons.meaning: When the starting price is above its usual level, the model's learned patterns pushed this forecast higher; this is a learned tendency, not a rule.

reasons.title: Price compared with recent averages
reasons.evidence: Same time last year: the latest price is 1.3% above its 7-day average and 8.0% above its 30-day average.
reasons.meaning: When a price sits above its recent averages, the model's learned patterns pushed this forecast lower.

explanations.what_it_means: The forecast is lower mainly because of the seasonal pattern in earlier years and the latest price being above its recent averages. However, the actual price may differ if supply or demand change.

scope.text: Prices are the median across the Maharashtra markets that reported each day, and arrivals are the total those markets reported, so arrivals also change with how many markets reported.

data_basis.text: Based on historical prices up to 2025-12-31, repeated for the same season and adjusted for inflation. No live market feed is connected, so this does not describe today's market conditions.

v3.method: SHAP values of the model are summed per group in log space; the predicted change in rupees is split in proportion: inr_g = start * s_g * (exp(L) - 1) / L, with L the model's log price ratio, so the group effects and the baseline drift add up exactly to the predicted change. Effects are on the starting price shown.

headline.text: About the same: the model's expected change for Cabbage (₹144) is smaller than its typical miss in backtests (about ₹420 per quintal at this distance), so no rise or fall is claimed.

banner.text: No 2026 market data yet — this forecast replays the same season of 2025.
banner.detail: The starting price is the 23 Oct 2025 price plus 5% for a year's inflation. Every figure below is dated from 2025 records.

cards.title: Seasonal pattern
cards.effect_text: Seasonal pattern pushed the forecast down by about ₹85.
cards.evidence: Cabbage: in 2024 the price changed -20% between 23 Oct 2024 and 17 Dec 2024; in 2023 the price changed -14% between 23 Oct 2023 and 17 Dec 2023 (average -17%).

agreement.text: In earlier years prices fell over this period, and the model pushed the forecast lower.

cards.title: Recent price trend
cards.effect_text: Recent price trend pushed the forecast down by about ₹20.
cards.evidence: Price on 23 Oct 2025: ₹1,300; +30% since 23 Sep 2025 (30 days) and +13% since 25 Jul 2025 (90 days).

agreement.text: The price has been rising recently, but the model pushed the forecast lower. The reason is not visible from the records shown.

cards.title: Supply (arrivals)
cards.effect_text: Supply (arrivals) had almost no effect on the forecast.
cards.evidence: Reported arrivals across the markets that reported, 24 Sep–23 Oct 2025: 388 a day (as reported), 19% below the October average of 2023 and 2024 (477 a day).

agreement.text: The model gave this almost no weight, so there is nothing to compare.

trust.baseline: starting price (reference-year price x 1.05, model ratio = 1)
lines: In 10,952 backtest forecasts for Cabbage, 31-60 days ahead, the average miss was about ₹420 per quintal (34%); the baseline “starting price (reference-year price x 1.05, model ratio = 1)” missed by ₹617.
The model beat that baseline here.
It called the direction right in 77% of the 9,735 cases where the price moved by more than 5% (28% of those moves were rises).
The 80% range contained the actual price in 79% of these forecasts (it should be about 80%).
warnings: These figures come from tests of the same kind of forecast (starting from last year's prices), which is less accurate than forecasting from current prices.

reasons: The model beat its baseline in both backtests and was not rejected in validation.
